key_insight: RL-trained LLM agents can learn spurious tool-use shortcuts—calling tools from superficial cues instead of real task need—unless tool necessity is explicitly rewarded.
engineering_relevance: For agent builders, this shows that robust tool-use policies require not just performance optimization, but reward design that penalizes unnecessary actions and checks decision-level necessity.
method: Build controlled synthetic QA and math environments with injected cue–tool correlations
Evaluate counterfactual cases where cues appear but the tool is not actually needed
Add a dense LLM-judge reward for each tool call based on whether the tool was necessary
evidence_signal: Across counterfactual evaluations, spurious tool invocation increased by up to 39%, and shortcut behavior appeared only after the agent had learned to use the target tool reliably.
watch_item: An LLM-judge reward may add cost and subjectivity, so its reliability and calibration need care when transferring to real-world agents.
paper_title: Spurious Tool Use: When RL Agents Learn the Wrong Reason to Act
